name: Tirumuruganathaswamy Temple, Tirumuruganpoondi
deity: Shiva as Tirumuruganathaswamy, with the goddess Avudainayaki (Muyangu Poon Mulai Ammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kongu country, sung in the Tevaram (8th century); present structure traditionally attributed to the Kongu Chola period
dynasty: Kongu Chola (traditional attribution) and later Tamil patrons
summary: Tirumuruganathaswamy is a Kongu Nadu shrine sung in the Tevaram, remembered for the day Sundarar, robbed of the Chera king's gifts by Shiva's own attendants in hunters' guise, sang out in protest and saw every treasure returned.

sections.history: Tirumuruganpoondi lies a few kilometres from Avinashi in the Kongu country of today's Tiruppur district, and is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines sung in the Tevaram. Tradition reckons it the second of the Kongu Nadu temples praised in the hymns, and its fame is bound to the saint Sundarar, who is said to have halted here on his way home from the Chera king. The temple that stands today is generally attributed to the Kongu Chola age, around the tenth century, though the sources are not firm and later patrons have certainly added to it. The village takes its name from Murugan, who by tradition worshipped Shiva here, so that the Lord is known as Tirumuruganathaswamy, the Lord worshipped by Murugan. Worship has continued within these walls for many centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple follows a modest Dravidian plan and, unusually for a shrine of this standing, has no towering rajagopuram over its entrance; one passes instead through a simple gateway into the walled enclosure. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga of Tirumuruganathaswamy, and the goddess Avudainayaki, also remembered by her Tevaram name Muyangu Poon Mulai Ammai, is honoured in her own shrine. A Vinayaka shrine recalls the part the elephant-faced Lord plays in Sundarar's story. On the walls, sculptures of the saint show him in three moods of the episode: anger, humiliation and joy.
sections.legends: Sundarar was returning with the rich gifts given by his friend, the Chera king Cheraman Perumal. Tradition says that at this spot he rested before the shrine of Vinayaka and did not go on to worship Shiva. The Lord, to test or perhaps to hear His devotee, sent His ganas in the guise of hunters, and the band took every one of the gifts. Bereft, Sundarar prayed to Vinayaka, who directed him eastward, and he then sang a hymn half of reproach and half of entreaty, chiding the Lord who lets His servant be plundered on the road. Shiva restored all that was taken. A second memory tells that Murugan, after slaying the demon Surapadma, dug a spring with his spear and worshipped Shiva here to be freed of that sin; a square stone beneath a neem tree nearby is said to be the guilt that left him. The accounts differ in detail, but the thread is constant: a Lord who plays with His devotees and always returns what He takes.
sections.festivals: The robbery of Sundarar is recalled each year in the Vedupari utsavam, the hunters' plunder, when the story is enacted with festive devotion. The Tamil month of Maasi (February to March) brings the annual Brahmotsavam, with Sundarar honoured in the festival. Maha Shivaratri is among the most prominent observances, and Pradosham is kept monthly as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Tirumuruganpoondi without haste. Enter the quiet enclosure, pause at the Vinayaka shrine as Sundarar once failed to do, and then go on to the sanctum of Tirumuruganathaswamy, afterwards turning to the goddess Avudainayaki. Look for the wall sculptures of Sundarar and read in his face the anger, the shame and the joy of that day. Devotees who have lost something, or who carry a worry they cannot name, come here with the saint's confidence that the Lord restores what is His to give back. The village is small and the temple is unhurried, and a visit sits easily alongside nearby Avinashi.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirumuruganpoondi lies close to the Tiruppur–Avinashi road, roughly 4 to 5 km from Avinashi and 7 to 9 km from Tiruppur, which has the nearest major railway station. Coimbatore International Airport is about 40 km away. Local buses and autos from Tiruppur and Avinashi reach the town; ask locally for the exact approach.
